title: Student Dissertations and Research Projects
text:
Preface
This book website is intended to offer resources for students working on dissertations or research projects. The content is based on various different handouts and files I created for students over the years.
The content provides general guidance only. For any assessment, you must always check the exact requirements provided in your class handbook or by the module leader to ensure you fulfill your specific assessment criteria.
The points covered here will apply to any general research project including short research papers, and undergraduate or postgraduate dissertations. The terms dissertation/project/paper will be used interchangeably throughout.

Zotero, mendeley, endnote
Have free and/or student versions
You can use these to keep track of literature you find, organise your notes, and automatically create your references.
You can use these for all your classes, but will save you so much time on big projects like this.

title: 2  Research Questions
text:
2.1 Coming up With Research Questions
Social scientists try to describe and explain different aspects of the social world. With this in mind, your research question(s) should communicate what you want to find out as clearly as possible. Research questions encapsulate what you’re doing, frame your project and inform hypotheses, methods, data collection etc.

title: 2  Research Questions
text:
2.2 Evaluating Research Questions

Make sure it is actually a question

‘The influence of media on voting’ is not a research question (or a question - needs to end with a question mark!)
Rephrasing this into an actual question will also help to force you to narrow down exactly what you want to find out: ‘How does UK news coverage of party leader debates influence public perceptions of competency?’



2.2.0.1 Don’t pick a question you already know the answer to


Real World Relevance

Topic should have consequences for real world political/social/economic issues
Most direct way is often when we can help understand something that effects many people’s lives, or predict/explain something that may be either harmful or beneficial



Scientific Relevance

Makes a contribution to a scholarly literature in order to increase our collective ability to construct scientific explanations of some aspect of the world
Directs attention to intellectual puzzles that remain to be solved, have not yet been posed, and the methods to solve them
Important to others, not exactly duplicating past research (though replication is valuable)



Clear & easily understood

Not too long, stay away from jargon as much as possible
Able to be understood by different audiences



Scope

Too narrow – not able to generalize to wider contexts, limited use to others
Too broad – unable to give concrete answers if problem is too abstract



Feasibility

Researchable in terms of time/skills/money required
Realistic in your given timeframe/deadline
Identify the appropriate methods needed to answer your given RQ
Potential funding/ethics approval issues



2.2.1 Sub-questions


2.2.2 Ways to relate topics to the existing academic literature

Attempt to provide evidence to one side of a debate within the current literature
Apply existing approaches to new contexts or time periods
Choose an area in the literature, of which no one has done a systematic study
Argue that an important topic has been overlooked, and begin a study of that area

title: 4  Structure of a Dissertation
text:
4.1 Example Structure of a Research Project
Dissertations should generally be structured in the same way as academic journal articles.
These are the different sections that you will typically see in a dissertation or research article:
Sometimes all of these sections may be present, sometimes only some of them will be. Different sections also might be much shorter or longer than others, or even not included at all, depending on what your research project is examining. Check your class handbook for your module to see what specific structure and format is required for your submission.
Common variations you will see might be:

title: 4  Structure of a Dissertation
text:
4.1.1 Title

A title that clearly defines your research topic.



4.1.2 Abstract

Brief summary of your research. A sentence each on; what you are looking into, how you did it, and what you found. Around 100-150 words.



4.1.3 Introduction

Background/context of the chosen topic.
Have a clear research question
Why the topic is relevant?


Real world relevance
Scientific relevance


Signpost what you will be discussing in the rest of the paper.



4.1.4 Literature Review

What is already known about the topic?
Is there consensus within the literature, or is it contested?
Do not just list everything that has been written on the topic. Only include relevant sources and ensure that you provide your own critical evaluation.
How does the existing literature relate to your own research?



4.1.5 Theory

What theories (potential answers to your RQ) have other studies came up with?
What degree of support/evidence is there for each theory?
Hypotheses

How can you turn these abstract theories/concepts into clear, testable hypotheses?
Think about framing your hypotheses in terms of your independent and dependent variables




4.1.6 Method

Why did you choose this method?
Case selection, sample size, sampling method
What are your independent/dependent variables? How can you measure them?
How you went about collecting/analysing the data
Any issues (measurement/sampling/missing data etc.)



4.1.7 Results/Findings

What did you find out? What patterns did you discover?
How does this relate to your hypotheses?



4.1.8 Discussion/Conclusion

Summarize your findings
What have your learned from your project?
Usefulness/limitations of your chosen method
How do your findings relate to the broader literature/wider society?
Potential areas for future research



4.1.9 Bibliography

Full references for all sources that are cited in the dissertation
Use the correct referencing system required by your assessment



4.1.10 Appendices

An appendix isn’t always required, but this is where you can include any supporting information for your project
This could be anything from: Your list of survey questions, the code used to run your analysis, additional figures or tables, additional information about your datasets.
